claims.text: Reactive SPS with an in-situ reaction can form a stable refractory HEA-Cu composite.
Rapid heating and short dwell times allow refractory elements to react and form a uniformly distributed intermetallic or solid-solution phase.
Rapid SPS processing prevents extensive elemental segregation associated with positive refractory-element/Cu mixing enthalpy.
The proposed starting material is a powder blend of refractory-HEA precursors and Cu.
The refractory elements have a strong positive mixing enthalpy with Cu.
Reactive SPS is applied to consolidate the refractory-HEA precursor/Cu blend.
High temperature, high pressure, and rapid heating trigger a self-sustaining reaction during sintering.
The proposed processing conditions limit excessive diffusion and phase separation.
A finely distributed interfacial reaction layer, consisting of an intermetallic or solid-solution phase, forms between the refractory phase and Cu matrix.
The interfacial reaction layer mediates microstructural evolution.
SPS permits the reaction to reach completion before long-range diffusion causes phase segregation.
Reaction-driven microstructural control overcomes the positive heat-of-mixing challenge and stabilizes the composite on a large scale.
The resulting composite will have a stable and uniformly reacted microstructure.
The resulting composite will retain high-temperature mechanical strength.
The resulting composite will retain irradiation resistance.
The Cu phase will provide effective thermal conductivity.
Conventional sintering or melting leads to phase inhomogeneity because positive refractory-element/Cu mixing enthalpy promotes segregation and unstable interfaces.
Inappropriate heating rates or dwell times can cause excessive diffusion or incomplete reaction and thereby compromise microstructural stability.
Phase-formation pathways and interfacial chemistries depend on the specific refractory-alloy composition.
